On a curated benchmark of 112 parameterized layout generation tasks using GDSFactory, SGLayout achieves a 76.79% pass rate, compared with 50.89% for the strongest baseline.

signals.title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery in PHP Web Applications
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25412v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain. We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent represents vulnerabilities and functional gadgets--intended program behaviors that can be repurposed in attacks--through preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection. It searches backward from unmet preconditions for capability producers and forward from discovered capabilities for functional gadgets that consume or amplify them. Object-centered chaining knowledge from our empirical study directs searches toward promising vulnerability classes, functional operations, and object accesses. We evaluate ChainAgent against Codex, a general-purpose coding agent, on 15 PHP applications across three shared LLM backends. ChainAgent achieves 42.02%--44.63% recall for goal-reaching components and recovers up to 4.4 times as many correct goal-reaching dependency edges as Codex. An additional evaluation of

signals.title: Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning for Mammography Vision--Language Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25418v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.

signals.title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25429v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

signals.title: Raptor: Rejection-aware Adaptive Tree based on Speculative Decoding
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25436v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tree-structured speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models (VLMs) by verifying multiple candidate continuations in parallel. However, long visual contexts increase the cost of speculative computation, making candidate coverage and redundant expansion important considerations beyond tree topology adaptation. We propose Raptor, a training-free framework that uses rejection feedback to jointly regulate candidate coverage and drafting effort. Our key insight is that acceptance length alone cannot distinguish insufficient candidate coverage from excessive deep expansion, and these conditions require different allocation decisions. Raptor therefore extracts complementary rejection-aware signals to characterize speculative progress, frontier coverage, and redundant expansion. These signals jointly guide bounded, momentum-smoothed updates of tree depth, branching width, and drafting budget, together with execution control that limits unnecessary drafting and progressively restores expansion when appropriate. Extensive experiments with two VLMs across seven multimodal benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Raptor, achieving up to 2.39x average speedup over autoregressive decoding.

signals.title: Demonstration-Free Skill Composition for Navigation and Manipulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25462v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning enables sequential tasks to be represented as compositions of separately trained skills. This paper evaluates demonstration-free hierarchical pipelines for MiniGrid navigation and robotic manipulation, comparing their training requirements and task performance with flat reinforcement learning baselines. The evaluation concerns complete pipelines with task-specific observation, reward and control structures. In navigation, two parameterised skills are reused across unseen FourRooms layouts under manually specified high-level plans. In manipulation, reaching, grasp alignment and lifting are trained separately, with downstream skills initialised from states collected during predecessor rollouts. Across unseen navigation layouts, the hierarchical pipeline substantially outperforms the evaluated flat DQN baselines while requiring fewer training interactions. In manipulation, the hierarchical chain requires fewer training steps than flat SAC and exhibits lower observed variation across seeds. The frozen Pick and Lift skills are further reused for stacking by training an additional Place skill.

signals.title: A Wolf in Sheep's Pixels: Visual Camouflage Attacks via HDR Gain Maps
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25469v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An image can pass automated safety checks while showing harmful content to its human viewer. We introduce DRJanus, a visual camouflage attack that exploits the gap between standard dynamic range (SDR) processing and high dynamic range (HDR) display. Automated systems often read only an image's SDR base, whereas HDR viewers reconstruct its appearance using an auxiliary gain map. DRJanus inverts this reconstruction to embed two independently chosen color images in a single JPEG, without querying or optimizing against the target model. It preserves the chosen SDR base exactly and reconstructs HDR targets at an average PSNR of 43.03 dB across 400 images. On a benchmark of 100 sexual-content images, DRJanus evades detection by all six tested commercial moderation services and nine vision-language models. Across five agents, each evaluated on 120 task cases per threat setting, attack success ranges from 31.67% to 100% for moderation evasion and from 95% to 100% for task manipulation. We also explore cross-view consistency checks as a mitigation. These findings expose a gap in visual trust: securing what a machine reads does not secure what a user sees. A demo is available at https://qshen0629.github.io/DRJanus/

signals.title: A four-level executable validation protocol for evaluating LLM-generated topology specifications of physics-based HVAC digital twins
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25471v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Physics-based digital twins of air conditioning, a principal energy consumer in manufacturing and buildings, can be generated automatically from a declarative specification of its equipment, connections, and sizing. Large language models (LLMs) now write such specifications from plain-language descriptions. Evaluations of these specifications stop at parse success, completed runs, or textual similarity, and cannot reject a model that converges in simulation but is physically wrong. In this study, a four-level protocol is proposed that tests whether an LLM-written specification not only executes but also yields a physically valid digital twin. Each specification is executed through static validity, model build, simulation convergence, and behavioral equivalence with a hidden reference model within bands calibrated by $\pm$20% sizing perturbations. The protocol was applied to eight LLMs and fourteen HVAC topologies, five describing an existing low-humidity test chamber. To test for authorship bias, engineers and a second model family also described six topologies. Within three repairs, seven of eight models built in 98.6 to 100% of trials, with simulations converging in at least 80.0%, but reached behavioral equivalence in only 50.0 to 98.6%. About half of the failed trials converged, but not to the reference steady state, mostly in desiccant rotor systems. Pooled pass rates varied by under five percentage points across description authors. These results imply that the physics hardest to model in each field, here the desiccant rotor, must enter the generation framework as validation levels. The protocol can be adapted to other fields that generate executable digital twins from declarative specifications.

signals.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25476v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring

signals.title: AIstatLab at BraTS-GoAT 2026 Task 3: Quality-Controlled Consensus Pseudo-Labeling and Dense Expert Adaptation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: BraTS-GoAT Task 3 evaluates brain-tumor segmentation across heterogeneous entities using shared ET, TC, and WT regions. We present a 3D ResidualEncoderUNet trained with quality-controlled consensus pseudo-labels, a training-only nested-region objective, and a four-expert bottleneck adapter. Five-fold ResEnc-M/L teachers gener ated predictions for 1,138 unlabeled cases; fusion, hierarchy enforcement, and confidence-and-agreement screening retained 983 for training with 1,351 annotated cases. The final five-fold ResEnc-M entry achieved mean DSC 0.834, mean NSD 0.510, and Acalc = 0.6720 on the validation server. Component effects were modest and region-dependent, with the clearest gains on ET. Source code is available at https://github.com/HeeSeung-Shin/Brats2026-Goat-HS.

signals.title: Planning Width Is Hard to Approximate Even Given the Unique Optimal Plan
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25484v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For each fixed $k$, iterative-width search finds optimal plans in polynomial time on tasks of bounded tuple-chain width, but the approximability of planning width has remained open even when an optimal plan is supplied. When all optimal plans visit the same state sequence, we characterize set and chain width as hitting numbers of competing states. We construct positive-precondition STRIPS tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan, a single reachable goal state, binary branching, and constant-size actions. Every reachable state lies on a goal-reaching execution at most one action longer than optimal, yet distinguishing width $1$ from $\Theta(N)$, where $N$ is the number of atoms, is NP-hard for set, chain, and goal-admissible width. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves a one-sided approximation factor $o(N)$ or a symmetric factor $o(\sqrt{N})$, and simple estimates attain both orders. For positive-precondition tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan of length at least two, testing set or chain width against a threshold $k\geq 1$ is coNP-complete for each fixed $k$ and $\Sigma_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete when $k$ is part of the input. Both results also hold for goal-admissible width if only one goal state is reachable. On an explicit state graph, a greedy algorithm approximates set width within a logarithmic factor even when optimal plans branch. Thus, knowing an optimal plan does not eliminate the difficulty of certifying substantially smaller width.

signals.title: Joint Language Modeling for In-the-Wild Speech-Scene Generation with Distinct Token Representations
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech-scene generation aims to synthesize intelligible target speech together with diverse environmental sounds as a coherent acoustic scene. The task is considered challenging in two respects. Speech and environmental audio differ substantially in their semantic and acoustic characteristics, yet existing approaches typically model the complete scene using a single mixed acoustic representation. At the same time, the two sounds are closely related in real-world speech scenes, whereas conventional approaches usually rely on simulated scenes mixed from independently recorded sources. We propose a large language model (LLM)-based framework for joint modeling of distinct speech and environment token streams. A source-aware neural audio codec extracts temporally aligned speech and environment tokens from mixed audio, and a pretrained LLM generates both token streams in an interleaved fashion conditioned on the natural-language scene description and speech content. This formulation preserves source-specific representations while modeling the token streams within a shared generative context. Since both streams are extracted directly from mixed recordings, the model can also be adapted to in-the-wild speech scenes without isolated sources. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves speech intelligibility, scene relevance, and audio quality over existing speech-scene generation techniques, with consistent gains from real-world adaptation. We further investigate the effects of distinct token representations and interleaved generation, and analyze whether the environmental sound remains stable while speech is active and how the two streams interact.

signals.title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25508v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.

signals.title: MATE: Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution for Safe and Efficient Mobile Control
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25526v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mobile agents on personal smartphones can affect private data, payments, settings, and the foreground screen. We present MATE (Mobile Agent Trustworthy Execution), an execution-layer system that controls the boundary between agent action proposals and device effects without modifying the underlying model. MATE represents each UI primitive as a structured action record that combines the instruction, target app, screen context, primitive, and action fields. Runtime Guardrail (RG) maps this record to an allow, block, or user-approval decision; Predefined Task Routing (PTR) serves recurring requests through verified routes with post-execution screen checks; and a floating interface keeps execution in a compact overlay. On MobileSafetyBench, MATE raises high-risk blocking from 29.7% to 97.0% under GPT-4o. On AndroidWorld, it reduces LLM calls by up to 6x and raises recurring-use task success to 95.7%.

signals.title: Learning Generative Ranking Policies for Whole-Page Optimization
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25527v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A recommendation page is consumed as a whole: the items on it compete for attention and complement one another, so the best page is not simply the individually best items placed side by side. We study whole-page optimization, which selects and orders the items on a page jointly to maximize the score of the page. The number of possible pages grows combinatorially, so good pages must be generated rather than enumerated. Some generative re-ranking methods use the same page-level training signal for every choice in a sampled page. Others imitate target pages built before training, which remain largely fixed as the generator improves. We address both limitations with one local page-level objective, which repeatedly moves the current generator toward pages with higher score. This objective splits exactly into one training target per position, and each target compares candidates at the same partial page by the scores of the complete pages they lead to. Every position therefore learns to choose the item that is better for the whole page, rather than the item that looks best on its own. We call this procedure whole-page policy improvement. On two public datasets, KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS-SeqSlate, which cover multi-objective item selection and constrained ordering, and on an industrial dataset of logged pages, our method outperforms the evaluated generative re-ranking baselines. On a synthetic benchmark with a known optimal page, it also comes closest to the optimum, showing that its improvements come from better whole-page decisions.

signals.title: CoachSI: Self-Improvement of Robot Policies with a Language Coach
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25529v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.

signals.title: Towards Autoregressive Neural Network Parameter Generation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25538v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently established a new paradigm in machine learning, demonstrating exceptional zero-shot generalization and complex reasoning capabilities. Concurrently, neural network parameter generation has emerged as a promising avenue for rapid task adaptation and model synthesis. Existing weight generation techniques, however, struggle to jointly learn the distribution of diverse models, to encode heterogeneous architectures within a single generator, and to generalize out of distribution. We therefore ask whether pretrained parameters can be encoded into a discrete domain so that the zero-shot generalization LLMs exhibit in text generation can be transferred to weight generation. Following this view, we propose an LLM-inspired approach, Instruction-Guided Parameter Generation (IGPG), that formulates network parameter generation as an autoregressive modeling problem. We first quantize pretrained weights with a VQ-VAE, then train a prefix-conditioned autoregressive generator over the resulting tokens. At inference, the generated weight tokens are mapped back to parameter space by the VQ-VAE decoder. We evaluate the framework across in-distribution generation, cross-dataset transfer, and cross-architecture settings. The proposed method achieves competitive performance in in-distribution generation and provides useful parameter initializations for held-out datasets and architectural configurations, improving downstream performance over random initialization after adaptation. These results suggest that discrete autoregressive modeling provides a promising framework for learning and transferring structure across collections of pretrained neural network parameters.

signals.title: The Coverage Selection Gap: Ranking, Not Generation, Limits LLM Rubric Construction
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25557v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Task-specific rubrics are increasingly used to evaluate open-ended language-model outputs, yet constructing comprehensive evaluation criteria from complex source documents remains challenging. We study automatic rubric construction in professional mergers and acquisitions (M&A) due diligence, where evaluation criteria must be inferred from task instructions and supporting documents without access to an expert-authored reference rubric. We introduce a multi-axis generation framework that explores complementary structural and free-form views of the source evidence to construct a broad pool of candidate evaluation criteria. To distinguish failures of criterion discovery from failures of candidate selection, we introduce the coverage-selection gap, which measures the difference between reference-free ranking and a reference-informed greedy diagnostic under a fixed selection budget. Developed on 16 tasks and evaluated on four held-out tasks, our framework achieves 0.876 macro recall against senior-authored reference rubrics under an LLM-based criterion-equivalence protocol. Ablation studies further show that introducing new structural search axes improves recall by 6-10 percentage points, whereas increasing generation volume along existing search directions yields at most 1.5 points. These findings suggest that, once a high-coverage candidate pool has been constructed, effective reference-free selection becomes a substantial bottleneck in document-grounded rubric construction.

signals.title: Online Mistake Detection in Instruction-Conditioned Procedural Video
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25567v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.

signals.title: FlashX: Scaling Robotic Experience Reuse for Embodied Agents with CBA-Based NAND Flash
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25580v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embodied agents are emerging as a promising paradigm for complex robotic tasks, leveraging Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) to generate actions through Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based iterative denoising. However, existing models often struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. We observe that retrieving successful experiences and using them to warm-start denoising enables agents to better adapt to unfamiliar situations while reducing computational overhead. This creates a new opportunity to improve task accuracy and inference efficiency simultaneously, in contrast to conventional acceleration techniques that trade accuracy for computation. However, realizing this opportunity requires scaling experience banks, introducing substantial storage and search overhead that challenges the capacity, bandwidth, and power constraints of edge systems. We propose FlashX, a CMOS Directly Bonded to Array (CBA)-based NAND flash architecture for scalable experience reuse in embodied agents. FlashX exploits CBA's high internal bandwidth for parallel pSLC key search, employing interleaved Compute-in-Flash (CIF) engines to sustain sensing throughput while retaining dense TLC latent storage. Proprioception-aware clustering further reduces search overhead and enables incremental experience acquisition without global reclustering. Evaluations across VLA and WAM workloads demonstrate up to 12.24\%p and 7.43\%p improvements in task success under dense and compute-efficient configurations, respectively. FlashX achieves 2.57$\times$ higher search throughput than the strongest prior NAND search architecture under pSLC sensing, with a further 9.7$\times$ search reduction through clustering. This de

signals.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25582v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.

signals.title: An Explainable and Scalable Hierarchical Tensor Framework for Integrating Multi-Omics and Digital Pathomics
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25584v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Background: Precision oncology requires integration of heterogeneous molecular and pathology data, yet many fusion models offer limited biologically grounded interpretability and struggle with missing modalities. Methods: We present Hierarchical Interpretable Tensor Fusion (HIT-Fuse), integrating six modalities: somatic copy number variation, DNA methylation, RNA sequencing, microRNA expression, RPPA protein abundance, and vision transformer-derived pathomics across four TCGA cohorts (glioma, lung adenocarcinoma, breast, and kidney cancer). Modality-specific autoencoders compress high-dimensional inputs, followed by two-stage CP tensor decomposition. Missing latent modalities are reconstructed using clinical covariates and observed omics to expand cohorts and retrain downstream models. A mathematical traceback mechanism enables global and local xAI attributions. Results: HIT-Fuse identifies distinct latent subgroups with significant survival stratification in glioma, breast, and kidney cohorts, both with complete and reconstructed modalities. Cohort expansion yields cohort-specific gains, including a 56.4% relative increase in weighted F1 for glioma. Biological validation against DepMap CRISPR screens, miRTarBase and RPPA annotations supports decoded drivers across all four cohorts. Essential gene rates range from 6.2% in glioma to 7.6% in lung cancer; example drivers include ANAPC11, SNRPD1, PLK1 and RPL14. Of decoded miRNAs, 71-92% have miRTarBase regulatory support, while 77-84% of selected genes are covered in DepMap. Conclusions: HIT-Fuse combines hierarchical tensor fusion, missing-modality reconstruction and traceable attributions to support interpretable multi-omics and digital pathology-based cancer prognosis ac

signals.title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25594v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.

signals.title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25597v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

signals.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25599v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-posi

signals.title: On the Informativeness of Structural Stability Bounds for GNNs: GINs versus GATs
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25603v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stability bounds for graph neural networks limit how much node representations can drift when the graph changes, but they are rarely compared with the simplest alternative: a bound on the distance between any two outputs, whatever the graph. We derive structural stability bounds for Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) and single-head GATv1 networks under deterministic edge perturbations that need not be small, and compare each with such a perturbation-independent diameter bound. For GINs, we characterize exactly when the stability bound is tighter, through a condition linking perturbation size, depth and maximum degree; it holds with a wide margin on Cora, but fails beyond a few layers on the low-degree MUTAG graphs. For GATv1, the bound is never tighter, which calls for analyses based on attention masses.

signals.title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25605v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

signals.title: Splice-Core: Low-Order-Bit-Splicing GEMM for Highly Energy-Efficient AI Inference Accelerators
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25617v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary (tub) hybrid general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that minimizes low-order accumulation latency, while retaining value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. Post-place-and-route INT4 yields 14%/9% smaller area for Splice-BP/Splice-LUT, compared to the systolic array.

signals.title: DAWN: Robust Neural Blind Deconvolution via Alternating Wiener Guidance
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25621v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Blind image deconvolution (BID) is an ill-posed inverse problem that aims to jointly recover a sharp image and blur kernel from a single degraded observation. Under nontrivial and high noise, which is common in photography and scientific imaging such as microscopy, BID remains particularly challenging, as existing methods suffer from noise overfitting and inaccurate kernel estimation. Existing training-data-free learning methods for BID, such as those based on the deep image prior (DIP), often utilize external guidance by including model-based estimates as additional loss terms, which underexploits the information these estimates carry especially under nontrivial noise. To address these challenges, we propose DAWN, a training-data-free DIP framework that alternates between injecting model-based estimates directly into the model input and refining this imperfect estimate with the network's own prior. To provide more reliable kernel estimates for these injections, we apply autoencoding regularization to both the image and kernel networks. On natural and scientific images under varying levels of Gaussian and Poisson noise, DAWN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both image and kernel quality (achieving up to +4.5 dB over the next best baseline on the Levin dataset at $\sigma = 0.1$). Without any training images, DAWN remains highly competitive with a state-of-the-art diffusion model on FFHQ, despite the latter being trained on a massive number of in-distribution images.

signals.title: AesDistill: Distilling Generative Aesthetics for Image Color Enhancement
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25635v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Image color enhancement aims to improve visual appeal, but previous methods often learn to reproduce ground-truth expert targets. These targets reflect the preferences of a few experts and cover a limited range of aesthetic choices. Matching them does not ensure stronger aesthetic quality across different tastes and scenes. By contrast, large generative models learn rich visual knowledge from large image collections and often produce vivid, appealing image edits. However, direct generation can change the source image's semantic structure along with its colors. In this paper, we introduce AesDistill, a framework for distilling generative aesthetics into image color enhancement. We use 4 leading open-source large generative models to produce 64,644 edited images as teacher targets at a cost of about 3,360 H100 GPU-hours, forming the AesDistill Dataset. AesDistill also includes AesDistill Student, a 1.13M-parameter model that learns teacher color changes through confidence-weighted supervision while preserving the source image's semantic structure. We evaluate AesDistill with 12 aesthetic and 4 image-quality assessment models. Every teacher's targets rank above the FiveK and PPR10K expert target means in the joint assessment. Across both datasets, AesDistill Student outperforms all 20 baseline methods and ranks directly behind the 4 teachers. These results demonstrate that distilling aesthetics from generative models enables a compact student to outperform methods trained on expert targets.

signals.title: Beyond Easy Clients: Difficulty- and Improvement-Aware Aggregation for Federated Reinforcement Learning in Robot Navigation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25637v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated reinforcement learning enables a fleet of robots to jointly learn a shared navigation policy without exchanging raw experience. In practice, however, the robots rarely operate in the same conditions: an open aisle is far easier to navigate than a cluttered room, and takes less learning to master. Standard federated aggregation rules ignore this. Uniform averaging weights every client equally, whether or not it is still learning, and weighting by episode return is worse, since easy environments permit high returns by construction. Both failures stem from what we call the \emph{plateau problem}: once a client masters its environment, its updates carry little new information even though its reported return remains high. We propose \emph{FedDIA}, which scores each client by how much its local training improves the global model it received, amplified by the difficulty of its environment. Difficulty is inferred from the model's own performance, without requiring any description of the environment. Both signals are measured against the global model, so they are comparable across clients. On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA reaches a mean success rate of $75.5\%$ across training and held-out environments, against $68.7\%$ for the strongest federated baseline. Its advantage holds when the models are transferred to hand-authored warehouse and living-space layouts, or when one of the clients is defective.

signals.title: Erasing the Wrong Thing: Conditional Attribute Leakage and Concept Erasure in Shared Foundation-Model Embeddings
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25640v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Medical-image embeddings are increasingly shared in place of raw images for authorized downstream tasks, yet they may reveal sensitive attributes. Standard concept-erasure methods target population-level guardedness. However, we prove that, when binary task and sensitive labels are associated, global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold while a nonzero linear task signal is preserved, so global erasure must either eliminate that signal or retain task-conditional linear leakage. We further show how global erasure affects linear readers' discrimination between positive and negative samples with different sensitive attributes, deriving an approximate closed-form prediction of its utility cost from pre-erasure statistics. Motivated by this conflict, we introduce Task-Conditional LEACE (TC-LEACE), a closed-form variant of LEACE that enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum of its fitting data. We evaluate four vision foundation models on 85 CelebA attribute pairs spanning a broad range of associations. After LEACE, conditional leakage persists across all four encoders, the discrepancy between marginal and conditional audits increases with association strength, and predicted utility costs track observed losses. We then examine hospital chest radiographs using three foundation models, including two biomedical models, in which chest-tube status is strongly associated with diagnosis. Although a marginal attack on LEACE-erased embeddings underperforms a diagnosis-only reference, chest-tube status remains detectable within diagnosis strata. TC-LEACE recovers most of LEACE's linear task-utility loss while keeping task-conditional leakage within a prespecified margin of LEACE's.

signals.title: DARSY: A Tool for Data-Driven Abstraction and Policy Synthesis for Stochastic Systems with Unknown Dynamics
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25654v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents DARSY: a software tool for abstraction-based verification and policy synthesis in discrete-time stochastic control systems with unknown dynamics and noise distributions. DARSY requires only a simulator of the system and a Lipschitz bound on its dynamics, and needs no knowledge of dynamics or noise distributions. The tool is fully automated and constructs a finite interval Markov decision process (IMDP) abstraction from sampled transitions, whose probability intervals are obtained via statistical techniques and Lipschitz reasoning. Robust dynamic programming on this IMDP then yields a policy together with a lower bound on the probability that the unknown system satisfies a desired specification. This lower bound holds with a user-specified confidence; that is, it is probably approximately correct (PAC). The tool is implemented in Python and supports general Lipschitz-continuous system dynamics and specifications expressed in syntactically co-safe LTL (scLTL), which includes reach-avoid and finite-horizon safety specifications as special cases. Beyond standard IMDPs, DARSY implements a two-layer IMDP (2IMDP) abstraction that also bounds the probability of transitioning to aggregated state blocks, yielding smaller abstraction errors than IMDP abstractions and, as a result, tighter satisfaction guarantees. We demonstrate DARSY's broad applicability across a variety of benchmarks and specifications.

signals.title: A$^2$-VLA: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Policies to New Tools through Agentic Affordance Discovery
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25656v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tools with different shapes can have similar functions, but transferring manipulation skills across tools requires understanding how tool geometry relates to the specific task and adjusting the manipulation strategy accordingly. The key challenge is to discover the common affordances that contribute to task completion across different tools and verify whether they support new tools in performing similar work. We present A$^2$-VLA, a tool-adaptation framework that combines an embodied agent with a VLA policy. It treats tool affordances as hypotheses the agent can construct, test, and revise. Given teleoperated demonstrations with a few source tools, the agent reconstructs the scenes in simulation and autonomously determines task-relevant affordance features: functional regions and their key geometric properties. It develops affordance-extraction skills and refines both the features and skills through autonomous experiments in the reconstructed scenes. Validated extraction skills accumulate in a reusable skill library for unseen tools. Finally, A$^2$-VLA uses encoded functional-region features as conditioning inputs to a $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone during training and inference. Evaluation examines affordance reliability in reconstructed scenes and real-robot task success on unseen tools. Our method achieves 86.1% success in simulated cross-tool trajectory retargeting based on affordances. On three real-robot tool-use tasks, A$^2$-VLA improves task success by 30.7 percentage points over $\pi_{0.5}$.

signals.title: GRODE-RTL: Source-Mapped Dependency Views for LLM-Based RTL Repair
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25661v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models show great potential for automated Register-Transfer Level repair, yet they struggle with non-local faults where root causes and failing outputs reside far apart in source code. Treating RTL as a flat token sequence obscures hardware dataflows, whereas exposing complete synthesized graphs overwhelms the model with fine-grained metadata. To resolve this representation dilemma, we propose GRODE-RTL, an anchor-centric representation that extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps netlist nodes back to editable source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view. By prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant hops, GRODE-RTL guides standard tool-using agents without exposing ground-truth hints or oracle feedback. We evaluate GRODE-RTL across 30 formally validated non-local faults using three LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3) alongside a controlled six-configuration ablation study. GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek, by 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and by 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on the hard-to-retrieve far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets of all three models. Our controls isolate structural relevance from generic context expansion, proving that selective dependency organization rather than full graph exposure is key to effective RTL repair.

signals.title: Beyond Entity Recognition: Vision-Centric Knowledge Visual Question Answering
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25680v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/VC-VQA.

signals.title: TipDex-VTLA: Learning When to Refine Actions with Touch for Dexterous Manipulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25683v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.

signals.title: From Geographic Memory to Spatial Generalization in Large Language Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25703v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can associate places with geographic descriptions, but recovering an observed association does not establish an ability to generalize across geographic space. We distinguish geospatial memory, the recovery of location--description associations observed during training, from spatial generalization, the prediction of descriptions for locations in unobserved regions. We investigate whether continuous location representations improve this generalization and encourage geographic knowledge to become spatially organized within an LLM. We frame this organization as a latent spatial field: a learned mapping from locations to descriptions connected through spatial dependencies. Building on a continuous spatial encoder, we project location representations into the model's embedding space and supply them as spatial tokens. We evaluate the resulting models on two newly curated geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London using two complementary assessments. Geospatial captioning tests both memory and spatial generalization by generating descriptions at observed locations and at locations beyond the spatial coverage of the training observations. A separate geospatial grounding model tests whether generated location--description pairs provide useful additional supervision for mapping text to geographic space. Across multiple LLM families, continuous location representations improve captioning at unobserved locations relative to textual coordinates, while their generated descriptions yield modest but consistent improvements in downstream grounding. Layer-wise probing and representation clustering provide additional evidence consistent with spatially organized geographic representations. Together, these fin

signals.title: STARK: Moving towards Personalized Agents That Truly Learn and Remember
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25705v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs.%, and silo knowledge within individual users. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

signals.title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25719v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.

signals.title: Verifying Before Enhancing: Target Evidence Chain Verification for Infrared Small Target Detection
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25724v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Infrared small target detection is essential for early warning, surveillance, remote sensing, and space-based target perception. However, infrared small targets are typically tiny, weakly textured, and boundary-blurred, making them difficult to distinguish from complex backgrounds. Moreover, target-like background structures can produce salient responses across multiple scales, making response strength alone insufficient for reliable target discrimination. To address this challenge, we propose VBE-UNet, a Target Evidence Chain Verification Network that assesses candidate reliability beyond response magnitude through complementary evidence cues. Specifically, counterfactual background explanation models local target evidence, while joint evidence verification integrates cross-scale support and perturbation-based contribution verification to guide feature recomposition. The resulting reliability estimates guide selective feature refinement, promoting target-relevant responses while reducing unsupported background activations. Extensive experiments on IRSTD-1K, NUDT-SIRST, and NUAA-SIRST demonstrate that VBE-UNet achieves superior detection accuracy and lower false-alarm rates compared with state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies and evidence reliability analysis further validate the effectiveness of the proposed verification framework.

signals.title: Auto-Alpha: A Framework for Autonomous Factor Research
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25732v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous factor research requires generating economic hypotheses as well as implementing and testing them. We present Auto-Alpha, a framework that connects report-guided initialization to self-directed research through a test-driven implementation loop. An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signal constructions; a research agent develops them with backtest feedback. Semantic audit, quantitative review, and human admission select factors for a persistent library, while an Experience Library retains research insights. Starting from 120 research reports, Auto-Alpha builds an initial library of 32 factors. It then generates new ideas and refines existing candidates, producing 420 implementations and retaining 62 additional factors. We evaluate factor quality and portfolio performance using a fixed library snapshot of 105 factors. The median 1-day Rank IC is 0.0301, and a weekly Top-300 portfolio returns 16.81% annualized after stated costs over 2020-2026, versus 1.71% for the CSI 1000 price index. These retrospective results document an operating research process and its artifacts; controlled evaluation is needed to isolate the contribution of its components.

signals.title: From Reliance to Overreliance: Taxonomizing and Detecting Relational Risks in AI Companionship
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Companion AIs are increasingly used for emotional support, yet distinguishing meaningful engagement from harmful reliance remains difficult. We introduce the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR), which operationalizes users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately identifies evidence of relational harm (RH), enabling empirical examination of when reliance behaviors co-occur with adverse consequences. Using naturalistic Character.AI and Replika conversations from 110 adults, we found EO-related behaviors in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations, while observable relational harms appeared in 10.5%. Although EO did not necessarily lead to harm, recurring patterns often co-occurred with harmful outcomes, suggesting value as risk indicators. Open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration. Qualitative analysis revealed expectations of care, repeated support seeking, dependency, distress, and reduced confidence in personal judgment. We argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to patterns and trajectories of EO-related behavior.

signals.title: PosteriorBench: Evaluating Behavior Posterior Sampling in Language Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25735v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rare language model behaviors can be difficult to study because obtaining them through ordinary sampling can require a very large number of samples. This motivates the behavior posterior sampling problem: given a language model and a behavior of interest, is there an algorithm that efficiently samples from the model's distribution over transcripts that exhibit this behavior? We introduce PosteriorBench, a benchmark for comparing algorithms by their compute cost and by how close their samples are to the true posterior in forward and reverse KL divergence. PosteriorBench contains 21 tasks on Qwen3.5-0.8B with behavior probabilities from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-1}$, each with exact posterior samples from a corpus of one billion labeled responses. We find that no method we evaluate is both efficient and faithful: simple methods like prompting are cheap but plateau at a high KL divergence from the posterior, fine-tuning on posterior samples is often cost-prohibitive, and several training methods from prior work do not perform better. Building a posterior sampler that can cheaply approximate the true posterior remains an open problem, and we hope PosteriorBench can measure progress towards this objective. Code and data are available at https://github.com/TransluceAI/PosteriorBench.

signals.title: An LLM-Driven Traffic-Control xApp for Dynamic 5G RAN Intents
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25736v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Programmable Radio Access Networks (RANs) enable runtime deployment of traffic-control functions, but selecting the appropriate configuration remains challenging as network conditions and service requirements change over time. Conventional solutions often rely on static rules or learning-based controllers with predefined state and action spaces, limiting their ability to accommodate changing intents. This paper introduces an LLM-driven xApp for traffic control in programmable RANs. The proposed architecture combines operator-defined service intents, runtime E2 interface telemetry, and the currently deployed configuration to generate traffic-management policies without blocking packet forwarding or the processing of incoming E2 measurements during LLM inference. Experiments on an OpenAirInterface 5G environment show that the proposed controller dynamically adapts the traffic-control pipeline to runtime intent changes, achieving an average intent satisfaction ratio of 0.91, compared with 0.52 for a static TC-RAN configuration. When channel conditions degrade, the controller maintains an intent satisfaction ratio of approx. 0.88, compared with approx. 0.4 for the static baseline.

signals.title: SAM 3 Sees More Than It Detects: Promptable Concept Maps Beyond Categories
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25747v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Promptable segmenters answer what a thing is. Dense prediction tasks also ask class-agnostic questions, such as what stands out or hides, how light is blocked, transmitted or reflected, and where structure lies. Robots, surveillance systems and image editors build on their answers. We study promptable concept maps (PCM), which extend SAM 3's promptable concept segmentation from noun instances to maps of concepts named by short noun phrases such as `"transparent object", with "none" as an answer. PCM-Bench groups the standard test sets of seven such tasks by the question they ask. On it, we find that SAM 3 sees more than it detects. Its semantic path responds to many of these concepts, yet a low image-level presence score can block every detection of its instance path. We present UNVEIL, which trains a copy of SAM 3's semantic path for these maps, with LoRA on copies of its last blocks. A separate presence decoder learns from verified negatives whether a concept occurs. With one text phrase per query, UNVEIL maps region concepts such as salient and camouflaged objects, shadows, transparent objects and mirrors. The same weights map thin structures such as edges and skeletons as well as object categories. Run next to SAM 3, it leaves SAM 3's own outputs unchanged. On each of the seven tasks, UNVEIL reaches the highest score among the compared promptable models, including SAM 3's official fine-tuning and pipelines built on multimodal LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/yuhuan-wu/UNVEIL.

signals.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25760v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer--agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, \NaturalPositiveShare{}\% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and Fai

signals.title: Closing Performance Gap for Diffusion Language Models under Low Inference Budgets
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25763v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.

signals.title: Collision-Free Is Not Enough: Passage-Conditioned Navigation for Wheeled-Legged Robots
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25788v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10{\deg} off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Glo

signals.title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25840v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUN

signals.title: LINEAGE: A Benchmark for Empirical Lineage Retrieval in AI Scientific Literature
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.25845v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Current research agents are moving beyond academic search toward literature synthesis and experiment planning.
