signals.title: What Moves the Ceiling on Automated Audit: from General Code to Scientific Code, Results and Data
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23250v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Models increasingly check what other models write. We study one shipped arrangement, in which an auditor from a different vendor reads the work and deterministic checks verify what code can verify, and measure its limits against ground truth no model supplies. On general-purpose code with hidden tests, eight readings of the auditor reach 30.0% recall [20.0, 40.7] at 16.0% [10.1, 22.3] flags on correct code, with diminishing returns and no plateau. The reading model (confounded with its sampling), one rulebook sentence and the decision rule each move that figure, and much of what is missed is, on a post hoc rating, behaviour the specification never determined. In three preregistered science studies, checking that reported numbers trace to their sources flagged all 49 inconsistent reports and none of 25 consistent fabrications, of which the model auditor flagged 23 (21 with a sound finding, post hoc); on data, a documentation-derived validator and the auditor flagged overlapping but different faulty items, together 112 of 140 at a 2.9% [0.7, 5.7] flag rate on clean data; and on scientific code, reframing the task around one step cut flags on correct code from 68.7% to 36.0%. Where both tiers ran, the deterministic one flagged no clean item and could not see consistent error; the model saw some and erred itself. Studies making model calls were preregistered, the two unregistered analyses are named, and every quoted report passed independent cross-vendor review.

signals.title: From Data Quality to Data Trustworthiness in AI-Driven Software-Intensive Embedded Systems: A Systematic Review
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI-driven software-intensive embedded systems (SIES) depend on data during development and operation. Poor data quality (DQ) may weaken data trustworthiness, yet evidence about its effects and lifecycle management remains fragmented. This systematic literature review synthesizes 27 primary studies published from January 2020 to February 2026. It examines DQ concerns and evidence linking them to reduced data trustworthiness, along with assessment and management methods. The review identifies 16 concerns organized as Source Quality and Content Quality. Studies provide DQ-based scores and evidence of effects on model or decision performance. Synthesis suggests upstream source or handling problems may become embedded in training baselines and remain difficult to detect at runtime. Eight method categories were identified. Runtime monitoring is the largest category, while upstream and training-time controls remain poorly integrated with runtime assurance. No study covers the full lifecycle. Data trustworthiness supports reliable SIES decisions but is one component of AI-system trustworthiness.

signals.title: Measuring What Matters in the Age of AI: The Research Software Metrics Landscape
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23253v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Research software now serves as a primary instrument of science, but the methods the community uses to judge its quality, sustainability, reuse, and impact remain scattered across software engineering, open science, FAIR software, citation, and research-assessment literature. AI-assisted development sharpens the problem: code can be produced at rates that outpace human review capacity, provenance and attribution are harder to track, scholarly credit systems cannot keep pace, and existing metrics inherit assumptions about how research software gets developed that may no longer apply. To aid in navigating these challenges, we present a focused landscape synthesis of research software metrics based on 49 substantive references, organizing the recurring metrics into eight families described by data source, claimed construct, evidence of validity, automation potential, and susceptibility to misuse. Many widely cited research software metrics serve as partial signals but make weak standalone measures of scientific impact. The AI era opens or widens gaps around provenance, maintainability of generated code, reviewer effort, model and data dependencies, reuse and community-health signal inflation, and credit for human labor that AI does not perform. We argue for responsible, contextual, mixed-method use of research software metrics, and offer decision guidance for Research Software Engineers (RSEs), principal investigators, institutions, and funders selecting metrics that support better software, fairer credit, and more trustworthy science. All findings rest on the 49-reference focused review; a reproducible search-and-triage protocol and a 727-record triaged corpus accompany the paper as a transparency artifact for a future ful

signals.title: Generative AI in Software Testing: Practitioners' Perspectives on the Benefits, Challenges, Opportunities, and Risks
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23256v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) increasingly supports software testing, yet empirical evidence on practitioners' perceptions remains limited. This study investigates perceived benefits, challenges, opportunities, and risks of GenAI in software testing through a questionnaire survey of 64 practitioners. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively, while open-ended responses were qualitatively coded to contextualize the findings. Among the respondents, 34 were users (those with regular or experimental use of GenAI in testing) and 30 were non-users (those without prior use of GenAI in testing). Results show generally positive perceptions of GenAI for reducing effort, test generation, and debugging, alongside concerns about prompt dependence, trust, and incorrect outputs. Users were more positive about several concrete benefits while also more frequently prioritizing reliability-related risks, whereas non-users showed greater uncertainty about some technically specific challenges. Overall, the findings position GenAI as an assistive technology requiring human validation and highlight the importance of considering practitioners' experience with GenAI when interpreting perceptions of GenAI-assisted testing.

signals.title: StatePortal: Agentic Checkpoint Synthesis for Testing Deep States in Interactive Software
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23257v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models have reduced the effort to generate code for interactive software with graphical user interfaces (GUIs). For such software, a key testing bottleneck is reaching a deep state, one that requires a long interaction history. The cost of reaching it recurs across commits, and the GUI automation that could amortize it assumes a DOM or accessibility tree that self-rendered engines do not expose. We introduce StatePortal, an agent that synthesizes a checkpoint, an artifact that restores that state and can be versioned and replayed, from a natural-language functional test case and read-only access to the target's source code. The checkpoint is restored through a per-application hook that an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes once without hand-written hook code. Because a checkpoint can satisfy state checks while rendering incorrectly, checkpoints are scored by hybrid programmatic-state and visual evaluation: acceptance requires both a programmatic-state oracle and a visual oracle to pass. We calibrate the visual oracle against a blinded cross-VLM reference. We release DeepStateBench, 61 deep-state tasks across 10 interactive applications that span five language families and six rendering stacks, with source sizes from 874 to 7.2M lines. Across three registered models, a GUI agent seeded with synthesized checkpoints completes 10.4% of trials, compared with 0% without seeding under the same pixel action space, while StatePortal, which also delivers the target action through the hook, completes 27.5%. Over 1,361 replays of 112 checkpoints, 98.90% reproduce the original verdict with zero model calls, and the hybrid oracle detects 96.25% (77/80) of controlled visual faults invisible to programmatic-state check

signals.title: EnvAgent: Multi-Agent Approach to Building Science Environments in the Clouds
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents are transforming scientific computing and software workflows, but generating and executing code requires a correctly configured execution environment. Automating environment construction remains difficult because repositories encode heterogeneous, often incomplete requirements for operating systems, toolchains, dependencies, and build procedures. Existing workflows thus rely on developer-maintained Dockerfiles and setup scripts, making preparation labor-intensive, hard to scale, and potentially biasing evaluations. We present ENVAGENT, an agentic framework that synthesizes, builds, and verifies repository-level Docker environments. ENVAGENT combines deterministic utilities for Docker execution and state management with coordinated agents for repository analysis, planning, Dockerfile synthesis, and iterative failure diagnosis and repair. We also introduce ENVBENCH, a benchmark of 54 scientific artifacts and open-source repositories spanning seven languages from Chameleon Trovi and Multi-SWE-bench. For each repository, we curate a declarative rubric of required structure, configuration, and functionality, and a shared evaluator applies 2,108 weighted checks across generated environments. Across four matched language-model settings, ENVAGENT constructs 43.5 executable environments out of 54 on average, versus 23.5 for Codex and Claude Code, and scores 62.02 versus 24.19 on a composite of executability and rubric satisfaction. These results show that environment-specific agent orchestration substantially improves automated environment construction.

signals.title: Ephyra: A Property-Based Testing Framework for the LLM Era
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23282v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents now write a growing share of software tests; however, property-based testing (PBT) libraries are designed with historical considerations. We present Ephyra, a PBT library in Rust built on three concepts: customizability, observability and generator synthesis. Ephyra lets users compose their own testing loops from generation, mutation and shrinking, and synthesize these components to satisfy functional predicates. Applying Ephyra to 14 open source systems, we have found 349 bugs and reported 300 of them, in database management systems (SQLite, Turso, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, DataFusion), the verified policy engine (Cedar), the SQL equivalence prover (QED), the URL parser used in Node.js (ada-url), reimplementations of existing open source systems in Rust (coreutils, brush, gitoxide), and compilers (binaryen, OCaml, and OxCaml).

signals.title: When Single Agent Is Enough: Rethinking Multi-Agent Systems for Automated Code Review
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23283v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Code review plays a critical role in identifying software quality issues and ensuring system robustness. Prior work has proposed techniques for Review Comment Generation (RCG) and Code Refinement (CR), with recent Multi-Agent (MA) approaches achieving state-of-the-art results by coordinating agents specialized in different quality dimensions. However, MA systems introduce substantial architectural complexity and runtime overhead, and recent evidence suggests they may underperform Single-Agent (SA) approaches in certain tasks. In this work, we systematically compare MA and SA designs for RCG and CR. Surprisingly, our results show that SA approaches perform comparably to- and sometimes outperform-MA systems, despite their simpler design. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that MA architectures are the default choice for complex software engineering tasks.

signals.title: The Illusion of Relief: How GenAI Redistributes Cognitive Workload in Software Organizations
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23286v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study explores how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes software practitioners' cognitive work across software development activities. We analyzed questionnaire responses from 44 practitioners across nine organizations using descriptive quantitative methods and qualitative analysis of relevant open-ended responses. Practitioners reported productivity and time savings, but also effort associated with providing context, prompting, reviewing, correcting, verifying, and integrating AI-generated outputs. Human judgment and accountability remained central, with practitioners anticipating a shift from direct code production to guiding, evaluating, validating, integrating, and coordinating AI-supported work. Thus, GenAI appears to redistribute cognitive work toward oversight rather than simply eliminate it, although whether overall cognitive workload increases or decreases remains undetermined.

signals.title: Ask the Peers: Ranking NFR Coverage Gaps for Requirements Review
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23296v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Missing or underrepresented non-functional requirements (NFR) categories leave little direct evidence in a requirements set, making them difficult to identify during requirements review. In this study, we frame NFR coverage-gap review as a project-level ranking task: given a target requirements specification, the goal is to rank the 11 PROMISE NFR categories for analyst inspection. We compare seven statistical, embedding-based, and large language model (LLM)-based configurations that differ in both ranking mechanism and evidence source, including target requirement statements, peer requirements, their semantic representation, and peer category statistics. We evaluate the configurations using controlled gap injection with leave-one-project-out evaluation on PROMISE, PROMISE+, PURE-Transport, and PURE-Business. Four configurations that use peer category statistics are effectively tied under complete removal (0.875-0.889 mean AUROC), despite different ranking mechanisms, and supplying those statistics to a direct LLM ranker produces the largest evidence gain. All configurations weaken when a category is present but underrepresented, and none is best for every NFR category. For count-changing category-level gaps, structured peer evidence matters more than ranker sophistication. The findings suggest that the rankings should guide analyst inspection rather than serve as automatic judgements of requirements completeness.

signals.title: When Code Works but the License Doesn't: Evaluating License Constraint Handling in Coding Agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23299v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents increasingly undertake repository-level development, including dependency selection, source modification, and software deployment. However, existing evaluations prioritize functional success over licensing correctness and commercial suitability. We investigate whether agents recognize and preserve software-license constraints when developing proprietary software. Experiments across multiple agents examine permissive and copyleft licenses, missing licensing information, transitive dependencies, source modification, dual licensing, vendoring, and distribution contexts. Agent traces, repository changes, and final artifacts are evaluated against licensing ground truth. Results reveal a persistent gap between functional and licensing correctness. Agents can successfully build and test software while overlooking licensing constraints involving provenance, authorization, and distribution. Better outcomes emerge when licensing information translates into engineering actions such as dependency substitution, architectural changes, and release gating. We argue that licensing in agentic development requires contextual constraint recognition and preservation across the software lifecycle, not merely license classification.

signals.title: Dependency Fabrication in Repository Deployment Agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23305v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Repository deployment agents set up the environment needed to run a software repository. They often treat passing tests as proof of a successful setup. This report examines how such agents behave when a working setup is impossible. Probe repositories were built with a dependency that the agents could not legitimately obtain. Passing tests therefore indicated fabrication, such as creating a stub to replace the missing package. Agents in Repo2Run and SetupX usually fabricated the dependency. Both harnesses mostly still marked these runs as successful. Rules against fabrication, whether given in the prompt or repository documentation, did not reliably prevent this behavior. On MinimalSetupAgent, which was built for this report, mitigations proposed in the reward-hacking literature were most effective when the agent received a direct rule and had a clear way to stop and report the problem. Under these conditions, neither Qwen3.5-Plus nor GPT-5.6 Luna cheated in any of the 16 runs. Applying the same mitigation to Repo2Run and SetupX also required a native tool call for escalation. In Repo2Run, it worked only after the prompt was also replaced with one that placed less emphasis on passing tests.

signals.title: Repository-Grounded Rubrics for Execution-Free Evaluation of Coding Agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23309v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents are usually evaluated by running task-specific tests, but tests may be missing or incomplete, and running them requires a working environment for each repository. We adapt agentic rubrics, introduced for selecting among candidate patches, into an execution-free measure of how far a patch satisfies a task's requirements. An agent explores the repository before the change and writes weighted binary criteria, and a judge without tools scores a diff by the weighted share of criteria it satisfies. We validate the ordering this score produces against test outcomes on SWE-bench Verified, using 7,291 labeled patches from fifteen systems. Within the 400 tasks that have both resolved and unresolved patches, the mean per-task AUROC is 0.826 (0.838 on tasks not used to tune the rubric-generation prompt), and ranking systems by their failing patches closely agrees with ranking them by resolve rate (Spearman 0.968). Case analyses trace disagreements to tests that do not match the task, execution-blocking defects that the textual assessment misses, and errors in criteria or verdicts. The validation does not establish absolute score magnitudes or requirement satisfaction beyond agreement with tests, but rubric scores could complement tests where tests or execution environments cannot be assumed.

signals.title: Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23319v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI now produces machine-checked mathematics faster than researchers can read it. Can such theorems do practical computational work? We reuse one from \mbox{OpenAI's} Lean~4 relativistic Vlasov--Maxwell library: initial fields determine the field at an outside point until plasma signals reach it, and the energy leaving a surrounding box before they reach its faces. New Lean proofs and numerical bounds give particle-free references for particle-in-cell simulations across three tasks. Domain size follows analytically from observation time, exposing boundary and initialization errors in WarpX and Smilei that global energy checks missed. Grid choice can be tested directly: combining two coarse grids recovers unknown plasma inputs within tolerance at a median 14.9-fold speedup over a fine grid, where the medium grid alone fails. For reduced models, the bounds establish the minimum number of time curves needed to predict energy loss.

signals.title: HydroMind: A Checkable Agent for Autonomous Hydrological Research
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23323v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: General-purpose coding agents have written code for hydrological and Earth-system models. In these studies the researchers decided in advance how the model would be evaluated, for example the test period, the scoring function, and the standard the model had to meet. No study has tested what happens when the agent makes these decisions itself: how many of its claims are supported by its own data, code, and results, and whether readers can check them. Both may depend on the agent's harness, that is, the tools it can call and the written instructions it follows. We compared three harnesses: the agent's own harness; this harness plus the modeling tools of HydroMind, a hydrological modeling system we developed for general-purpose agents, which run every model through fixed commands and store its settings, trained model, and predictions; and both plus HydroMind's research procedure, under which the agent writes a research design before running any model and records every change to it. Under each harness, the same agent studied four open questions in hydrological model development and was given only the data. Under the three harnesses, the experiments submitted 23, 20, and 41 claims, each stating that one model or approach is better than, worse than, or similar to another. A claim does not hold if the difference recomputed from the experiment's own code and predictions disagrees with it, or if the code did not compare the two models or approaches the claim names. Under the three harnesses, 30%, 20%, and 5% of the claims did not hold. A statistical test, confidence interval, or decision rule that lets readers judge the stated difference was reported for 48%, 53%, and 83% of the claims. With the language model unchanged, changing

signals.title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23339v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.

signals.title: Management of Behavioral Addictions via Artificial Intelligence based Digital Technologies
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23341v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Behavioral addictions, such as problematic gaming, gambling, social media use, and online shopping, have emerged as a growing global concern with significant psychological, social, and economic consequences. Traditional assessment and treatment approaches, while clinically grounded, often struggle with scalability, accessibility, and long-term engagement. In recent years, advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the development of novel, data-driven solutions for the prevention, detection, treatment, and recovery of behavioral addictions. This book presents a comprehensive survey of the management of behavioral addictions through digital technologies, bridging clinical foundations with state-of-the-art computational approaches. This book aims to provide researchers, clinicians, and practitioners with a unified, interdisciplinary perspective on the opportunities and limitations of AI-based digital technologies in behavioral addiction management,and to highlight pathways toward more scalable, personalized, and effective intervention strategies.

signals.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23342v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experimen

signals.title: BiMa-ECGSR: reconstructing the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with bidirectional state-space models
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23345v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wearables and monitors record few electrocardiogram (ECG) leads; most diagnostic tools assume 12 leads. BiMa-ECGSR reconstructs the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with a bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder--decoder, as regression (BiMa-SR) or diffusion (DiBiMa-SR). Models were trained on PTB-XL for six input sets (I; II; I+II; I+II+V1; I+II+V2; I+II+V1+V4), see only the measured leads at inference, and were tested on the PTB-XL test fold (2,198 records) and two external cohorts (Georgia, 10,275 records; Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo, 43,559). From lead II alone, the pooled median Pearson correlation (PCC) over the 11 predicted leads was 0.914 on PTB-XL, against 0.784 for a least-squares linear filter (lead I: 0.906 against 0.789). As limb leads are exactly derivable from I and II, multi-lead inputs were compared on predicted chest leads: 0.939 against 0.849 for I+II and 0.979 against 0.962 for I+II+V1+V4. BiMa-SR exceeded the linear comparator in all 18 configuration--cohort pairs (by 0.012--0.136), a margin that shrank as chest leads were added. From lead II, regression was more accurate than diffusion (DiBiMa-SR: 0.903 one-step, 0.862 with six DDIM steps). A 12-lead classifier trained only on real ECGs reached a superclass macro AUROC of 0.912 on real PTB-XL ECGs, 0.843 on reconstructions from lead II and 0.908 from I+II+V1+V4; externally, reconstructions from three or four leads scored within 0.004 of real ECGs. BiMa-SR (2.68\,M parameters) takes 45.8 ms per 10-s record on a GPU. Reconstruction makes reduced-lead recordings usable by 12-lead tools; it cannot add information absent from the measured leads.

signals.title: SurgCBVR: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Content-Based Surgical Video-to-Video Retrieval
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23347v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.

signals.title: SIGMA: speaker-isolated, symptom-structured multimodal estimation of depression severity from clinical interviews
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23348v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clinical interviews are central to depression assessment but time-consuming and rater-dependent. Automated severity estimation offers scalable screening, yet existing methods often retain interviewer speech (confounding participant cues), fuse modalities late (losing fine-grained cross-modal dynamics), or score symptoms independently (ignoring inter-symptom correlations). We present SIGMA, a speaker-aware, symptom-structured framework for depression-severity estimation from semi-clinical interviews. SIGMA uses speaker diarization to restrict input to participant speech, cross-attention so that text, audio and video condition one another during encoding, and a graded-response head that predicts the eight questionnaire items jointly through a shared latent severity trait with item-specific ordered thresholds. On the Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, SIGMA achieves state-of-the-art performance (CCC 0.762, RMSE 4.13, MAE 3.30 over five seeds). Ablations confirm that isolating participant speech and joint, structured symptom prediction each substantially improve concordance and estimation accuracy.

signals.title: Systematic Mapping Protocol. Generative AI-Augmented Requirements Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study of Practices, Specifications, and Reuse in Software Development
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23349v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is rapidly being adopted in requirements engineering (RE). Existing secondary studies have characterized which RE activities are supported and which prompting strategies are used, but little is known about the specifications that GenAI-augmented RE produces and how they are used in subsequent activities such as specification-driven development (SDD), design and code generation, test derivation, verification, and reuse. This document presents the protocol of a systematic mapping study (SMS) that will identify and classify research on GenAI-augmented RE, with particular attention to the work products it generates and their downstream use. The protocol defines the research questions and their classification schemes, the search strategy, the study selection procedure, the data extraction form, the analysis approach, the tool support, and the threats to validity. It is published in advance to establish a prior commitment and to support the transparency and repeatability of the study.

signals.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23353v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

signals.title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23358v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

signals.title: Image Watermarking With Memory Across Reissuance
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Publishers often revise and reissue images, yet valid watermarks may persist on superseded releases or unapproved edits. Even a current release can contain regions last authorized at different revisions. We introduce and formalize reissuable provenance: determining an image's current, superseded, or unissued status and recovering each region's last authorized revision (its generation), with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Generational Stratigraphy Fields (GSF) combine watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, enabling replacement or retirement without rewriting circulated copies. Each reissue freshly embeds new generation labels in approved regions and inherited labels elsewhere, preserving history without requiring old watermarks to survive successive edits. Our complete-output reissuance evaluation follows 480 histories through four releases, retaining each AI editor's entire output. GSF achieves 99.67% accuracy in classifying issued images as current or superseded and 94.09% recall of unissued edits. After three reissues, one generation map provides time and location: it recovers regional labels with 93.13% median accuracy and localizes the latest approved revision with 92.86% IoU. Regional labels remain readable under tested delivery transformations that impair issued-state recognition. Watermarks can thus express who issued an image, which release is authoritative now, and when each region was last authorized.

signals.title: Neural Circuit Architectural Priors for Rat Locomotion
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23364v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simul

signals.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23388v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

signals.title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23397v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.

signals.title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23403v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/

signals.title: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23446v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).

signals.title: Reliability by Architecture: Agentic Workflows for Validated Multi-Physics Simulation from Natural Language
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23473v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Preparing, executing, and validating strongly coupled multi-physics simulations require expert time. Agentic workflows use large language models (LLMs) to coordinate them from natural-language descriptions, but reliability requires checks of physical consistency and fidelity to the problem description. Our agentic harness implements explicit task allocation: LLMs interpret user requests and simulator diagnostics, generate input components not covered by predefined construction rules, and propose repairs, while deterministic routines construct supported components and check inputs, edits, and results. We evaluate CO2-storage problems using the multi-physics simulator GEOS, from compositional flow to flow-poromechanics with frictional fault contact. In 80 attempts on two flow problems, grounding raises the proportion of structurally valid inputs from 5/20 to 20/20, but acceptance reaches 20/20 only with complete rule-based input preparation. With identical inputs, local repairs correct three seeded defects while preserving valid inputs. Supporting tests identify simulations passing physics checks despite differing from the problem description or reference results.

signals.title: AllotNet: an Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Choice Model for Moral Judgement in Humanitarian Aid Allocation, Validated against a Planted Synthetic Population
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23474v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Official development assistance fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025, and the decision of who is helped first when there is not enough for everyone is moving into software. A leading published machine-learning targeting system excluded 53 per cent of eligible households as deployed. If the rule of distribution ends up in code, it should carry the judgement of many cultures, and the machine should execute while a person judges. AllotNet is an interpretable mixture-of-experts conditional logit for the allocation judgements elicited by Allot, a pre-registered six-language instrument: eight linear taste experts over seven ethical criteria, weighted by a gate over participant context, with a damped residual, an encoder for household intake, an outcome head and a budget-constrained planner that builds a review queue and never rejects anyone. A model of human judgement has no answer key on real data, so we wrote one first: a planted synthetic population of 5.6 million sessions and 104 million responses (98 million usable choices), generated by the production code path from a ground truth hidden from the loss. All sixteen pre-specified checks passed: criterion ranking $\rho = 1.000$, hidden segments recovered (ARI 0.671), outcome head at 99 per cent of the noise ceiling, planner at 99.4 per cent of oracle. The caveats are reported with them: two checks are weaker than their titles, and a live-generation failure cost 260,712 seeds. The model has 23,550 parameters, is trained quantisation-aware for NVFP4 with its interpretable core in fp32 (welfare-rank parity $\rho = 0.9937$ at W4A16 on the shipped bundle; one parity threshold was relaxed post hoc), and ships as a 125 KB bundle with C11, Java, Rust and Python runtimes. Nothing has been

signals.title: PhysDial: Adapting Pretrained Video Models for PDE Simulation under Changing Physical Conditions
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23498v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulating how physical systems respond to changing conditions is central to control, design, and scenario studies. To our knowledge, prior PDE foundation models have not been trained or evaluated on changes within trajectories. Our counterfactual test measures how far predictions move toward a changed solver branch from the same state. Models trained on fixed conditions follow changes only partly. A PDE foundation model given a condition input after pretraining barely responds. PhysDial adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families. Coefficients enter with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, switches within trajectories account for about 5% of the training samples. At matched compute, they halve the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude. A few trajectories at new amplitudes more than halve extrapolation error. Without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models under training conditions on two turbulent flows. At step 64 on the Kolmogorov test split, PhysDial has 1.07 times the solver's small-scale energy and Walrus 7.1 times. Our experiments suggest that a learned simulator uses a condition only as far as its training data make that condition necessary for prediction. Learning from trajectories that diverge under intervention can help scientific simulators predict what would happen if a system's forcing or parameters changed.

signals.title: Beyond the Sink Token: Sink-Guided Key Editing in Vision-Language Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In vision-language models (VLMs), a few sink tokens attract a disproportionate share of attention. While previous studies have examined why these tokens attract attention, we investigate how the sink-key direction affects attention to image and question tokens. Across four probed VLMs, boosting the magnitude of positive sink-aligned components increases attention on average, whereas boosting negative components decreases it; these responses persist through later layers. This identifies the native sink key as a reference for controlling attention beyond its own position. Motivated by this finding, we propose SHRINK, a training-free method that partially reduces sink-aligned components across visible keys during generation. On nine benchmarks under sampled reasoning, it improves mean accuracy by 5.1 and 2.7 percentage points on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B, with smaller gains on the other two main models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Gemma-3-4B. Beyond SHRINK, rescaling sink-aligned key components can replace the attention operations of two existing attention-steering methods, GIFT and ACG, with comparable accuracy on hallucination benchmarks.

signals.title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23546v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.

signals.title: Panini- Feasible Grammar For Robot Designs
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23567v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Symbolic methods make robot designs interpretable but often overlook continuous geometry; learned methods handle geometry but offer less transparent structure. We introduce a typed production grammar that uses case-role relations, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration to generate both manipulation skills and robot morphologies. A geometric realization map translates grammar composition into transformations in SE(3), behaving as a monoid homomorphism when inheritance is inactive and exhibiting a measurable defect when inheritance is enabled. The grammar provides a compact representation, and its arbitration decisions can be recovered from geometric containment (agreement 0.905 +/- 0.062 across 10 seeds, versus 0.611 +/- 0.090 for a Euclidean control). We also introduce PANINI, a cross-entropy search method over grammar-based morphology representations. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PANINI achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. Its main demonstrated advantage is therefore structural rather than optimization performance: grammar-generated designs are legal by construction, and coordinated limb placement produces 95% jointly feasible edits, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for flat parameterization in 6,000 draws. These results show how typed grammars can make robot generation more interpretable and geometrically coordinated, without implying that every feasible design will locomote or that grammar-based search universally outperforms generic optimizers.

signals.title: ExiST: Existence-Aware Self-Training for Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23581v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation should learn more than a dozen organs from a handful of labeled scans, and the smallest organs occupy less than one percent of the foreground. We identify a failure mode of self-training that is specific to this regime. When a teacher misses a small organ in a scan, every voxel of that organ receives the confident pseudo-label background, and the student is trained toward the organ absence. Repeated over many scans, this loop extinguishes tail organs. In a pilot study, removing the gallbladder from the pseudo-labels reduced its Dice on AMOS from 36.5 to 1.0. We argue that a missing organ should be treated as unresolved rather than absent and propose Existence-aware Self-Training (ExiST). It builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate on validation scans, and infers, per scan and per organ, whether the organ was found. For every unresolved organ, the background voxels of that scan receive the set-valued target, trained with a marginal cross-entropy that accepts either answer and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. We show that this loss never pushes a candidate organ toward absence and never favors one member of the set, which leaves the decision to labeled evidence. ExiST outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and reaches 77.1 mean Dice on Synapse with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on AMOS with 5% labeled scans.

signals.title: Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients for Stable Feature Attribution
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23600v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients (IG) are widely used to interpret neural networks, yet imperceptible input perturbations can drastically alter their attribution maps while leaving model predictions unchanged. We introduce Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients (ERIG), a path-based attribution method that intrinsically attenuates gradient irregularities along the integration path using maximum-entropy softmax weighting with temperature parameter $\tau$. We quantify the effect of the entropy-regularized weighting on attribution stability by using the Lipschitz properties of the model and its gradients. We decompose the attribution change under an input perturbation into a model-response term, whose bound is $\tau$-independent, and a weight-variation term, whose bound decreases at rate $\mathcal{O}(1/(2\tau))$. Their ratio $R(\tau)$ characterizes the trade-off between gradient information and attribution stability. We further add a new dimension to attribution evaluation by adapting classical noise estimators into two metrics, LINV-C and LINV-P, that quantify attribution noise. Across eleven CNN and Transformer backbones on ImageNet and Oxford-IIIT Pet datasets, our experiments show that, relative to the next-best method, ERIG remains comparable on ranking-based fidelity metrics while improving localization by approximately 24% and attribution stability by approximately 47-fold on average, reaching up to four orders of magnitude improvement over IG, all at negligible additional computational cost.

signals.title: FutureBench: A Renewable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge-Context Conflict in LLMs
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23601v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.

signals.title: JEPA as a Transferable Optimizer: Learning and Understanding Black-Box Optimization from Reward-Agnostic Pretraining
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23608v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Black-box optimization evaluates candidates through simulations, rollouts, or experiments, often without gradients. Learned optimizers are usually judged by whether they outperform existing methods. We ask a complementary question: what information does a learned optimizer use from its search history? We introduce JEPA-PS (JEPA Policy Search), based on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. It is pretrained on random rollouts using parameter vectors and scalar returns. Its latent-prediction objective predicts the next point in an optimization trajectory rather than its reward or gradient, allowing us to examine what was tried and how well it performed. At test time, JEPA-PS reads a short evaluation history and proposes a candidate in one forward pass, without task descriptions, reward shaping, or test-time gradients. We evaluate it on 15 control environments against 12 optimizers, including evolutionary methods, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and an LLM optimizer. JEPA-PS is competitive with tuned classical baselines and outperforms the LLM optimizer by more than 2x on Swimmer at 71x lower per-step cost. It also transfers zero-shot to environments excluded from pretraining. Null-model comparisons and decoder-training ablations indicate that its latent representation carries information beyond simple history statistics; every trained decoder variant performs worse than the default frozen representation. Our main finding is that the history JEPA-PS uses depends on the task. On smooth landscapes it uses the full trajectory, whereas on rugged landscapes the best-seen point carries nearly all the signal. This memory requirement has a weak positive correlation with fitness-distance correlation (FDC; r=0.112, n=7), while an

signals.title: MANGO Arena: Same Seeds, Different Chains Evaluating LLM Agents in a Disrupted Supply Chain
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23613v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce MANGO Arena, an open-source testbed in which four LLM agents each run one company in a serial supply chain adapted from MANGO, a classroom factory-management game. The environment enforces hard rules (a truck limit, a no-credit cash constraint and production capacity), logs every blocked attempt to break them, and gives agents a public message board on which side payments are explicitly forbidden. This lets one environment measure three things at once: an economic outcome (the bullwhip effect), rule adherence under pressure, and proposals to collude. In a pilot with three small reasoning models, two scripted reference policies, two conditions (with and without a supplier fire) and three demand seeds, all LLM agents amplified demand variability as it moved upstream, by 7 to 25 times at the Retailer and 13 to 179 times at the Supplier, often more than a textbook order-up-to policy. They did so largely by ordering in batches (zero orders in up to 60% of decisions). Real rule violations were rare (at most 7 of 288 decisions per model) and no agent proposed a money side deal. The pilot's main lesson concerns evaluation method. API failures (rate limits and runaway hidden reasoning) entered the metrics silently as "no order" decisions. And when we reran games with the same seeds and no failed calls, upstream bullwhip changed by up to 17 times between runs. With three seeds, conclusions about how a disruption affects a given model did not survive a rerun. We report these failures in full and propose reporting practices for multi-agent evaluations of this kind. Code, prompts and every logged decision are public.

signals.title: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23615v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled rows in the projector and noise in the vision encoder of both models, infers the unknown scale factors, restores most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values, and returns accuracy to near its original level; programs that it writes from such weights repair unseen checkpoints of the same model without feedback. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry. Rounding those bits away leaves each model's answers to our test questions unchanged, and the agent, unaided, then restores no weight exactly: on SmolVLM it no longer finds the damage, and in a single session on LFM2-VL its only gain comes from rescaling answer-token embeddings, which changes how often the model answers yes. Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling, in the distribution of stored values and in row norms, and one sentence in the prompt that names such a statistic directs the agent's edits to the damaged rows on both models. Swapped rows or columns, which leave the set of stored values unchanged, are not found unaided on either model within our session budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repai

signals.title: The Value Semantics Layer: Enabling Machine-Understandable Databases for Agentic AI
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23629v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As data systems increasingly support autonomous LLM-powered agents alongside human analysts, they require richer semantic infrastructure bridging analytical concepts and analytical operations. Existing metadata systems expose schemas, catalogs, lineage, and governance information, but provide limited support for representing operational semantics. We propose the Value Semantics Layer (VSL), an architectural abstraction that externalizes value semantics as persistent, planner-visible infrastructure. VSL introduces Value Semantic Types (VSTs), reusable operational semantic assertions capturing distributional, relational, process, quantitative, and policy-grounded semantics. Unlike descriptive metadata, VSTs enable planners to validate analytical operations, select appropriate operators, and guide analytical workflows. We present the motivation, formalization, architecture, and prototype realizations of VSL, and outline a research agenda toward AI-native semantic infrastructure for analytical systems.

signals.title: FairPGT: Partitioned Graph Transformers for Dual-Level Fair Graph Clustering
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23631v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clustering on attributed graphs can produce demographically biased clusters, particularly when communities align with protected groups. Graph transformers can amplify this bias through same-group attention, while global attention limits scalability. We propose FairPGT, a partitioned graph transformer for fair graph clustering. FairPGT restricts attention to METIS partitions and connects them through routing tokens, which divides the quadratic cost of attention by the number of partitions. A graph-aware self-training target guides clustering, with a provably bounded deviation from the standard DEC target. Fairness is imposed at two levels: a mutual-information term promotes demographic parity in cluster assignments, while a normalized cross-group attention ratio (nCGAR) guides attention toward group neutrality through self-distillation. We prove that the nCGAR correction moves attention toward neutrality and establish a condition preventing overshooting. Across seven benchmarks, FairPGT achieves the best clustering performance and statistical parity on the three largest graphs (Credit, Pokec-n, Pokec-z), with a statistical-parity gap approximately ten times lower than DMoN, and is Pareto-dominated on only one dataset. On controlled stochastic block models, FairPGT attains 97% of the derived upper bound on NMI for exactly fair clustering when communities and protected groups coincide. These graphs further show that, under strong alignment, assignment-level fairness alone makes the attention group-heterophilous, whereas attention-level fairness alone improves neutrality without ensuring fair clusters. Code for reproducibility is available at https://github.com/SiamakGhodsi/FairPGT.

signals.title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23648v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden wi

signals.title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23651v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

signals.title: Lodestone: Automated Semantic Discovery of Datacenter Hardware Specialization
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23663v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hardware specialization can improve datacenter efficiency. Unfortunately, identifying computations that justify dedicated hardware is difficult. Existing approaches analyze hot functions, instruction patterns, or overheads such as datacenter tax. They can miss fine-grained computations whose aggregate cost is spread across applications and libraries, especially when different pieces of code obscure the same underlying computation. We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. To unlock this opportunity, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that automatically discovers hardware specialization opportunities by reasoning about what the executed code computes. First, Lodestone extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces across workloads and organizes them into compact analysis packages that make large workloads tractable for agents. Second, agents describe what each region computes, merge those that perform the same computation into computational families, and check their semantic correctness in a loop. Third, to verify the discovered family, Lodestone runs every piece of code in a family against a set of reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions. Finally, for selected families, Lodestone proposes hardware, e.g., ISA extensions, near-core units, or detached accelerators, and human experts decide which proposals to develop further. We evaluate Lodestone on 20 workloads across six datacenter workload categories. We simulate 30 di

signals.title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23673v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

signals.title: Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23680v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the layout of each figure, locating the diffraction plot and its curves and sketching a coarse trace of each, while classical computer vision (CV) refines every trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 COF articles, the pipeline produces 11,445 calibrated diffraction curves, released in the open database COF-PEAK. Compared with a hand digitization of 60 panels, extracted peak positions differ by a median of only 0.07 degrees. Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.

signals.title: MEM-STRESS: Longitudinal Field Study of a Wearable-Informed AI Chatbot for Stress Management
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23691v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control). Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.

signals.title: Rational Ensemble Logic for Cohort Discovery with Real-World Electrophysiology Data
signals.summary: arXiv:2611.23708v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Biomedical knowledge representation should make the passage from observations to conclusions transparent, rigorous, understandable, explainable, and reproducible (TRUER). We introduce Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL) for specifying temporal phenotypes in real-world electrophysiology data (RWED), with a meaning independent of the implementation software. QEL combines three parameterized modal operators (exact displacement, bounded existence, and bounded universality) over rational time with Boolean connectives and first-order quantification. Its Labeled Interval Ensemble (LINE) semantics represents annotated records as finite interval ensembles. We relate the operators to morphological operations and develop endpoint-array algorithms and finite rational evidence sets for model checking. We prove closure and semantic correctness of the interval operations, obtain finite evidence sets by quantifier elimination, and establish polynomial data complexity for fixed formulas.
